question: According to the Digital Services Act (DSA), Member States should refrain from adopting or maintaining additional national requirements on matters falling within the scope of the DSA, as this would affect its direct and uniform application. However, this should not preclude the possibility of applying other national legislation applicable to providers of intermediary services where the provisions of national law pursue other legitimate public interest objectives than those pursued by the DSA. 1.
Does the Commission agree that Member States could legitimately adopt national legislation to regulate online wildlife trade specifically for conservation or animal welfare objectives?

Most of the DSA provisions do not apply to providers that qualify as micro or small-sized enterprises as defined in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC. Does the Commission agree that national legislation could be legitimately adopted by Member States to regulate online trade by providers that qualify as micro or small-sized enterprises as defined in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.4.2024) The Digital Services Act (DSA)1 fully harmonises the rules applicable to intermediary services with the objective of ensuring a safe and predictable online environment for citizens to trust digital services and business to grow and thrive across the EU single market.
It addresses, among others, the dissemination of illegal content online through specific due diligence obligations for intermediaries.

In view of the full harmonisation of the DSA, Member States should not adopt or maintain additional national requirements on matters falling within the scope of this regulation: the contrary would cause legal uncertainty and regulatory fragmentation which would go against the objectives of the DSA.

This does not preclude national legislation that regulates wildlife trade for conservation or animal welfare, insofar as it does not cover the elements already governed by the DSA, and it complies with EU law2.

In this regard, the Commission notes that national rules aimed at defining due diligence obligations of online intermediaries with a view to preventing the dissemination of illegal content, even if limited only to certain providers or to some specific type of illegality, would actually pursue the same objective of the DSA and they would thus be pre-empted by the full harmonisation provided for in this regulation.

To the contrary, national rules aimed at ensuring that wildlife trade qualified as illegal would not fall under the DSA. The DSA exempts micro- and small-sized providers from several of its obligations in order to keep the regulatory burden proportionate to the risks.

Such objective would be limited, and the harmonising effect of the regulation would be endangered, if national laws could impose similar or diverging obligations to the providers benefitting from that exemption.
1 As set out in Articles 1 and 2 of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA), and as further clarified in Recital 9;
